samples.text:
Crime is a serious problem in every society, and prisons are one way to deal with it. Some people believe prisons should mainly punish criminals, while others think they should help prisoners to become good citizens again. In this essay I will discuss both views.

People who support punishment believe that criminals must pay for what they did. If someone hurts another person or steal their property, it is fair that they lose their freedom. Also, hard punishment can stop other people from committing crimes because they are afraid of going to prison. Victims and their families may also feel that justice is done when the criminal is punished strictly.

On the other hand, many people think that rehabilitation is more important. Most prisoners will return to society one day, so if they learn nothing in prison, they may commit crime again after they are released. If prisons give them education and job training, they can find a work and live normal life. For example, a prisoner who learn to be a mechanic or a cook has a better chance to get a job. This is also cheaper for government, because keeping people in prison costs a lot of money.

In my opinion, prisons should focus more on helping prisoners to change. Punishment is necessary, but it is not enough to solve the problem of crime. However, for very dangerous criminals, protecting the public should be the first priority.

In conclusion, although punishment is important, I believe that prisons should mainly help offenders return to society, because this reduce crime in the long term.
samples.why: Addresses both views with a clear opinion · relevant ideas but limited depth · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and article errors (steal, find a work, this reduce) that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Societies differ in how they view the purpose of prison. Some people believe that its main function is to punish those who break the law, while others argue that prisons should concentrate on rehabilitating offenders so that they can return to society as law-abiding citizens. I believe that while punishment has its place, rehabilitation should be the primary goal.

Those who see punishment as the main purpose argue that justice requires offenders to suffer consequences in proportion to the harm they have caused. Victims often feel that a harsh sentence acknowledges their suffering, and the public expects serious crimes to be treated seriously. In addition, supporters of this view claim that the threat of an unpleasant prison experience deters potential criminals. If prisons are seen as too comfortable, they argue, this deterrent effect may be lost.

On the other hand, advocates of rehabilitation point out that the vast majority of prisoners are eventually released. If they leave prison with no qualifications, no job prospects and the same attitudes that led them to crime, there is a high risk that they will reoffend. Education, vocational training and counselling can give former prisoners the skills and confidence to build a new life, which ultimately protects the public more effectively than punishment alone. There is also a financial argument, as reducing reoffending lowers the enormous cost of repeatedly imprisoning the same people.

In my view, the loss of freedom is itself a significant punishment, and time in prison should be used constructively. Although some dangerous offenders must be kept away from society for long periods, even they should be given opportunity to change.

In conclusion, while punishment is a necessary element of any justice system, I believe prisons should focus mainly on rehabilitation, since this is the most effective way to reduce crime and make communities safer.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended and supported · logical organisation with clear central ideas · good topic vocabulary (reoffend, deterrent, vocational training) · mostly accurate structures with one article slip.

samples.text:
How a society treats those it imprisons reveals a great deal about its values. One view holds that the principal purpose of prison is to punish offenders for their crimes; another maintains that prisons should prioritise preparing inmates to return to society as law-abiding citizens. Although punishment is an unavoidable element of imprisonment, I would argue that rehabilitation should be its central aim.

The case for punishment rests on principles of justice and deterrence. Many people feel that those who inflict harm on others deserve consequences proportionate to their actions, and that a sentence perceived as lenient fails to respect victims. It is also argued that the prospect of a harsh prison regime discourages potential offenders, and that prioritising prisoners' welfare sends the wrong message about the seriousness of crime.

However, this approach has significant limitations. Since the great majority of prisoners are eventually released, the question is not whether they will rejoin society but in what condition. An offender who leaves prison without skills or support, and with stronger links to criminal networks, is highly likely to reoffend, creating new victims and returning to custody at great public expense. Rehabilitation programmes, by contrast, address the underlying causes of offending, whether a lack of education, unemployment or addiction, and thereby offer more lasting protection for the public. Moreover, the deterrent value of harsh conditions is questionable, as many crimes are committed impulsively or by people who do not expect to be caught.

For these reasons, I believe that the deprivation of liberty should be regarded as the punishment itself, and that time spent in prison should be used to reduce the likelihood of future offending. This does not mean ignoring the need to protect the public from genuinely dangerous individuals, but even in such cases the goal of reform should not be abandoned.

In conclusion, while punishment has a legitimate role, prisons best serve society when they focus on rehabilitation, as this ultimately leads to fewer crimes and fewer victims.
samples.why: Both views thoroughly explored and critically evaluated · well-argued, qualified position · excellent logical progression · wide, precise vocabulary (deprivation of liberty, custody) · wide range of complex structures, error-free.
